content_items.title: Collaborative Development of an Institution-Wide Controlled Vocabulary

programme.title: Collaborative Development of an Institution-Wide Controlled Vocabulary
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract:
Developing an institution-wide controlled vocabulary presents significant organisational and technical challenges. At the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, a Controlled Vocabulary (CV) Working Group was established to harmonise terminology used across the institution. Recent digitisation efforts and migration to a shared Collection Management System (Specify) revealed inconsistencies in terminology and object description practices across subcollections, limiting interoperability and discoverability.

Over a two-year period, the CV Working Group developed an institution-wide controlled vocabulary through an iterative process. Initial focus groups identified requirements and consolidated existing terminology lists into a preliminary thesaurus. A key factor in the project’s success was the structured coordination of stakeholder involvement. Internal presentations and regular communication with collection managers and other interested parties helped build institutional support for adopting the CV and updating collection records. Domain expertise from collection staff was essential to refine the vocabulary and ensure that it remained accurate and applicable across subcollections. Following the distribution of the preliminary vocabulary, participants were invited to review and refine term definitions.

The CV has since been integrated into institutional digitisation workflows, and its ongoing maintenance is now embedded in collection data management practices at the museum. This case study highlights the importance of collaboration and iterative review in the implementation of institution-wide vocabulary standards.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the chair as the first speaker ('Caitlin Thorne'); content matches the abstract. Includes about five minutes of audience Q&A.

content_items.summary: Caitlin Thorn, a data manager at the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, described how an interdisciplinary working group built a shared controlled vocabulary for about 30 million objects whose sub-collections used different terms for the same thing (object type, preparation type, availability). Instead of a dedicated thesaurus system they chose a structured Excel spreadsheet: collection staff already know Excel, and the list can move to a dedicated system later. The work ran from January 2024 workshops through a Collection Cafe presentation and specialist review to implementation as Specify pick lists. Q&A covered hierarchies, whether the list will be shared, governance, and alignment with Darwin Core.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A shared vocabulary across a large museum depends as much on familiar tools, trusted forums and ongoing governance as on the terms themselves.
content_items.why_it_matters: Many institutions migrating to a shared collection management system hit the same terminology problem. This talk gives a low-tech, people-centred recipe that others (Naturalis said it is about to try the same) can reuse.
key_points: Collections used different terms for the same thing, or the same term for different things, e.g. for object type, preparation type and availability.

A thesaurus was treated simply as a list of terms with definitions; the group's main effort went into writing disambiguating definitions (e.g. 'lost' means permanently gone, 'missing' means it may reappear).
Commercial thesaurus systems were evaluated, but a structured Excel sheet (English, German, Latin where relevant, definitions in two languages) was chosen for accessibility.
The internal weekly 'Collection Cafe' forum and institution-wide emails were used to build participation and credibility.
The final vocabulary was aligned with Darwin Core lists and implemented as Specify pick lists, with a process for requesting changes.
The group has no authority over collections: nearly every term a collection asked for was included, and only ambiguous terms were negotiated.

notable_claims.claim: The museum holds around 30 million objects whose collections developed different ways of describing themselves.
A simple Excel spreadsheet was chosen over dedicated thesaurus systems because collection staff already know Excel and it can be migrated later.
The vocabulary was implemented in Specify pick lists and aligned with Darwin Core.

recommendations: Use familiar tools to lower the barrier for collection staff to contribute.
Use a trusted existing forum to give the project visibility.
Plan ongoing governance, not just the initial term list.
results_findings: A consolidated, bilingual institution-wide vocabulary with definitions, implemented in Specify pick lists and used in the new data portal.

q_and_a.question: Do terms have hierarchies and how are they modelled in Excel; will the lists be published? (Naturalis)
q_and_a.answer_summary: Three sheets: terms, list names, categories; no deeper hierarchy was needed. Published internally only so far, but they can share it.

q_and_a.question: How does governance work if collections disagree or feel their needs aren't met?
q_and_a.answer_summary: The group has no authority over collections; nearly all requested terms were included and only ambiguous ones negotiated; a change process exists.

q_and_a.question: Did you reuse existing external controlled vocabularies?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Internal lists were compiled first, then checked against Darwin Core lists; German minimum information standards still need checking.

representative_excerpt.text: We also think that ongoing governance matters just as much as creating the initial term list, so not leaving the project once the list is created, but we've established a way for people to stay in contact with us and for us to develop the list in the future.

notable_moments.description: Decision to use an Excel spreadsheet instead of a dedicated thesaurus system.
Disambiguating 'lost' versus 'missing' in the availability vocabulary.
Lessons learned on compromise, familiar tools, trusted forums and governance.

content_items.title: From Silos to Standards - Advancing Standardised Collection State Documentation for Institutional Continuity and Coordination

programme.title: From Silos to Standards - Advancing Standardised Collection State Documentation for Institutional Continuity and Coordination
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract:
Collection-specific knowledge often lies exclusively with collection management staff. While collection managers understand the state of the collections they oversee, this information rarely reaches decision-makers or data managers in a standardised form. In South Africa, many institutions lack dedicated data managers, and those that do often lack access to collection-related contextual information needed to prioritise digitisation workflows and support data compliance.

Standardising collection state documentation addresses these challenges on three fronts. Operationally, institutions gain visibility into collection conditions and priorities, improving resource allocation. Institutionally, the system creates institutional memory that persists beyond staff turnover, preserving knowledge and collection history for future staff. Strategically, a shared standard introduces a common vocabulary that enables siloed institutions to move beyond isolated problem-solving toward coordinated, community-based approaches.

In 2025, we launched a prototype system across partner institutions using Google Apps Script and Google Data Studio. Although engagement varied, the pilot validated the concept. However, maintaining the system, onboarding collections, capturing data through Google Forms, and manually configuring dashboards proved labour-intensive and difficult to scale.

To address these limitations, the prototype was refactored into a standalone web application that streamlines collection state documentation and reporting workflows across institutions. The system supports institutional continuity while enabling a more standardised approach to collection management in South Africa.

speakers.name: Jacobus Christiaan Steenkamp
speakers.affiliation: National Science Collections Facility (NSCF), South Africa

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Christiaan Steenkamp from the National Science Collections Facility in South Africa'; content matches the abstract. One audience question.

content_items.summary: Christiaan Steenkamp described how South Africa's NSCF supports a network of about 23 partner institutions, many without data managers, in documenting the state of their collections. Tacit knowledge about readiness, risk and conditions usually sits with individual staff. A 2021 community collection management and conservation manual led to a national collection assessment. Its first tracking tool, built on Google Forms, Apps Script and Looker Studio in 2025, was then refactored with agentic development into a standalone system. The new system scores implementation, documentation and risk, links specimens to jars, preservation batches and storage conditions, enriches records from GBIF with IPT-ready export, keeps audit trails and generates handover documents. It works alongside Specify and BRAHMS.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Standardising how collection state (readiness, risk, conditions) is recorded turns tacit curatorial knowledge into shared, comparable institutional memory.
content_items.why_it_matters: Collection state and curatorial history are largely missing from current standards. This work shows how a national network with thin staffing can capture them, and it points to a gap beyond Latimer Core.
key_points: The NSCF network covers about 23 partner institutions, from full teams to single staff members, built over nine years.
Darwin Core describes occurrences and Latimer Core describes collections, but collection state, readiness and risk are not captured in shareable form.
A community collection management and conservation manual (2021) led to a national assessment scored with taxon experts and observers.
The first Google Stack tracking pipeline (Forms, Apps Script, Looker Studio) was view-only, tedious to update and hard to scale.
The refactored system scores implementation, documentation and risk, lets institutions customise questions, and uses role-level security.
It links specimens to jars, preservation batches, fluids and environmental conditions, keeps an audit log and generates customisable handover documents for staff continuity.
GBIF data can be pulled in, edited with tracking, and exported in IPT-ready format; the system works alongside Specify and BRAHMS rather than competing with them.
questions: What is a collection state, and what does it mean for a collection to be 'ready'?
Do institutions have formal processes for collection state or informal notebook habits?

notable_claims.claim: Many institutions in the NSCF network have no data managers at all.
Collection state, readiness and risk are not captured by Darwin Core or Latimer Core and often live only in individuals' memory.
The Google Stack pipeline was refactored into a standalone system using agentic development.
The biggest standards gap is defining what a collection state is; Latimer Core is basic for this purpose.

future_work: Pilot the refactored system with some institutions, then broaden to the whole network.
Formalise and publish the collection-state vocabulary (implementation, documentation, risk).
Contribute collection state to curatorial history within the extended specimen.

q_and_a.question: How does this compare to current TDWG standards and the new Darwin Core Data Package; what are the key gaps?
q_and_a.answer_summary: He stayed within Darwin Core where possible; the biggest gap is Latimer Core's basic treatment of collections and the lack of a concept of collection state and readiness.

representative_excerpt.text: But where the big gap here is, is what is a collection state? What does it mean for a collection to be ready?

notable_moments.description: Tacit knowledge: 'We can know more than we can tell' (Polanyi) applied to collection state.
Scoring of implementation, documentation and risk in the refactored system.
Handover documents to preserve institutional memory when staff leave.

content_items.title: Bridging the Gap: Strategies for Integrating Person Identifiers into Collection Databases

programme.title: Bridging the Gap: Strategies for Integrating Person Identifiers into Collection Databases
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract: Unambiguous identifiers for person names are critical for research based on collection data. Every specimen in a collection is the result of human agency - through collection, preparation, description, and curation. Identifying these agents enhances data quality by referencing the source of intellectual authority, by resolving collector networks or by providing additional insights into the history of collections. While identifier management workflows have existed for decades, Wikidata has become a central broker for biodiversity-related identifiers. The introduction of the “collection items at” property (P11146) in 2022 enabled the seamless linking of collectors to holding institutions in Wikidata. In less than four years, over 47,000 items (i.e. unambiguously identified persons) have been assigned this property, showcasing a significant cross-disciplinary community effort. Despite this progress, the integration of unique identifiers into primary collection databases remains slow. This process requires deep domain knowledge, identifier management expertise, and, most crucially, significant time. This creates a fundamental bottleneck: collection curators possess the necessary knowledge and access but lack the time to prioritize integration, whereas the broader community has the capacity for disambiguation but lacks access to institutional records. This presentation will delve into the process of person name disambiguation, exploring possible solutions that can decouple the workflow and enable collections curators to benefit from community-curated databases like Wikidata. By understanding these challenges and implementing strategies for collaborative data enrichment, we can enhance our ability to leverage human agency within biodiversity collection data.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as an online talk by 'Frederic Berger', deputy head of the Collection Future programme at MfN. Played as a pre-recorded presentation; the chair noted he was not yet in the Zoom room and could be asked questions on Whova. No live Q&A.

content_items.summary: Frederik Berger set out a still-conceptual strategy for linking person name strings in MfN collection data to persistent identifiers via Wikidata. About 30,000 people in Wikidata are linked to collections via property P11146, around 15,000 have Bionomia IDs and 13,500 are referenced from Entomologists of the World. MfN's own data yields about 800,000 name occurrences, 200,000 distinct strings and roughly 13,000 clusters, suggesting about 15,000 people. Only about 1.6% are currently linked to a PID in the central CMS. He compared prioritising frequent names against complex clusters, and proposed a web names directory that reconciles against the collection-related subset of Wikidata, with experts making the final decision.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Wikidata's community-built person data can be used to pre-structure candidate matches, but expert judgement and institutional priorities remain essential for identifying collectors.
content_items.why_it_matters: Agent disambiguation is a major bottleneck for linking specimens. The quantified gap, prioritisation options and restricted-reconciliation idea are directly reusable by other collection-holding institutions.
key_points: No specimen exists without an agent; Wikidata can broker links between institutional databases and other collection information.
About 30,000 Wikidata humans are linked via 'collection items at' (P11146); about 15,000 people with Bionomia IDs and 13,500 from Entomologists of the World are also represented.
The MfN WikiProject 'MfN Berlin Names' (led by Sabine von Mering) lists about 1,100 people.
MfN name data: about 800,000 name strings from about 30 tables, deduplicated to about 200,000 and clustered into about 13,000 groups, suggesting about 15,000 people.
Only about 1.6% of people in the central CMS have an unambiguous PID (about 10% if distributed lists are included).
About 1,500 agents account for up to 90% of collection objects, so prioritising frequent names maximises impact; tackling complex clusters improves authority data quality instead.
Next step: a web-based names directory mapping clusters, strings, sub-collections and candidate Wikidata QIDs, reconciling only against people already linked to collections.

content_items.title: Confronting legacy data for primary type specimens

programme.title: Confronting legacy data for primary type specimens
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract: Often historic natural history collections pose great challenges such as tracking taxonomic changes between the database and the physical labels, properly recording specimen movements, and maintaining legacy databases. This is particularly true for the SI NMNH Entomology Department, which is home to ~150,000 primary types. In 2007, data was migrated from INQUIRE, a database designed by the department, to EMu, a Collection Information System (CIS) used museum wide. Due to structural incompatibilities of INQUIRE with EMu, the data migration faced challenges and significant nuances of INQUIRE data were lost. All type records migrated from INQUIRE were categorized as “INQUIRE TYPES” in EMu and publicly flagged, while new type records were categorized as “Entomology Types”. From the time of the migration, the department tried to remedy the lost nuance by updating INQUIRE Type records whenever a type was handled. Dubbed the Type Inventory Project for Entomology Specimens (TIPES) Project, Collections staff are working alongside Curators to reconcile primary type specimen records in EMu against registration files and the physical collection, while maintaining a list of what should be physically present. The project has created opportunities to redefine workflows and ensure proper data capture, physical specimen security, and legal accountability, while sharing up-to-date records online and on GBIF to mitigate future data loss. The goal is to develop a streamlined workflow that removes communication barriers and prevents bottlenecks from forming on any one role. Additionally, the department is exploring AI-driven tools to identify gaps in the Primary Type collection via automated literature reviews for keywords, compared against the existing known inventory after its completion.

speakers.name: Cailin Meyer (name as transcribed; spelling uncertain)
speakers.affiliation: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Entomology

actual.identification_notes: Presented by a colleague of the programmed speaker Jessica Bird, who could not attend at the last minute. The presenter handles transactions and acquisitions; the chair introduced her as 'Cailin Meyer from the Smithsonian' (later 'Kaelin'/'Kaelyn' in ASR), and before the session she said she was presenting for 'Jessica Horn' (ASR for Jessica Bird). content_items.summary: The presenter traced the USNM Entomology primary type catalogue through handwritten ledgers (since 1896), the in-house INQUIRE type database (1980s), CRIS (mid-1990s) and EMu (migration 2007, full use by 2011). Poor field mapping from INQUIRE meant every migrated type record carried a public disclaimer as an 'INQUIRE type'. Migrated CRIS transaction records lacked objects and had odd dates. Barcodes were duplicated, and some types were never catalogued or linked to acquisitions. The department launched a multi-year, 100% specimen-level type inventory: curators compare EMu spreadsheets with specimens, and transaction discrepancies are resolved against paper records.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Decades of database migrations left the second-largest insect collection's type catalogue unreliable, and only a full physical inventory is fixing it.
content_items.why_it_matters: The talk is a frank case study of how legacy migrations degrade data and what a sustained, phased remediation looks like. Collections facing similar INQUIRE/CRIS/EMu-style histories can learn from it.
key_points: The USNM Insect Collection (est. 1881) holds about 35 million specimens, over 400,000 species and over 130,000 primary types, with a small staff.
Type ledgers in use since 1896 recorded catalogue number, name, sex, locality, year, sender, collector and entry date.
INQUIRE (1980s, in-house) was kept separate from CRIS; both were migrated to EMu in 2007, and INQUIRE fields mapped badly.
All migrated INQUIRE records carry a disclaimer until reviewed; a 'complete' record needs review, a USNM ENT barcode and an image.
Other problems: uncatalogued types, duplicate barcodes from an external printer, and workflow gaps leaving acquisitions unlinked.
Phase 1: curators check EMu spreadsheets against specimens. Phase 2: transaction linking and loan matching. Phase 3: vetting INQUIRE data and type citations. Phase 4: imaging.
Progress: almost 3,500 existing type records completed and over 500 new types added.

content_items.title: From Legacy Database to Cloud: Challenges in Migrating Legacy Collection Data to a FAIR Collection Management System

programme.title: From Legacy Database to Cloud: Challenges in Migrating Legacy Collection Data to a FAIR Collection Management System
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract: Natural science collections play a vital role in scientific research, yet they often rely on outdated legacy databases that reflect years of curatorial practices. At Senckenberg German Entomological Institute, these collections are currently managed across Corel Paradox relational databases and additional spreadsheets, each with customized schemas and specific entomological terminology. However, only 22,470 of our estimated 3,800,000 specimens are accessible through the GBIF Global Registry of Scientific Collections. The lack of standardization, interoperability and accessibility restricts the potential of our valuable collection data for biodiversity research. We present a working example of our approach and processes to migrate heterogeneous data into the DINA Collection Management System. We identify three key challenges in this migration process. First, we must reconcile inconsistent database schemas and curatorial terms with DINA's data model, which is closely aligned with the Darwin Core standard. Second, we must tackle data quality issues that arise from maintaining a legacy curation tool, for example, outdated taxonomic names and discrepancies with public taxonomic backbones, such as the Catalog of Life. Finally, we must coordinate efforts across different institutes within Senckenberg, each with unique schemas, curation workflows and institutional cultures. By completing the migration to DINA, we anticipate achieving FAIR-compliant, identifier-based collection data that enhances accessibility and usability through GBIF and for researchers worldwide. We aim to demonstrate how data managers can bridge collection management expertise and new digital infrastructure to implement data migration projects that meet FAIR standards.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Marije Timmermans from the Senckenberg Institute'. The chair said 'Mönchengladbach', probably an ASR/intro error for Müncheberg, where SDEI is based. Talk focuses more on her role as the institute's first data manager than on migration specifics.

content_items.summary: Marije Timmermans, the first data manager at SDEI (since February 2026), described preparing for migration to the DINA collection management system, which Senckenberg's central Data and Modelling Centre implements across eight institutes. SDEI's five entomology sub-collections use separate Corel Paradox database instances with diverging schemas, plus card catalogues and personal spreadsheets. Collection data is treated as a management tool rather than research infrastructure, and there is no formal data governance. She acts as liaison, runs one-on-one sessions and workshops, and proposes mappings. Her working method is design-thinking prototypes that domain specialists test.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A dedicated data manager who acts as liaison and uses iterative prototypes can make a small institute's move to a shared CMS workable despite fragmented legacy practices.
content_items.why_it_matters: It shows the organisational side of CMS migration: divergent schemas, missing governance and the value of empathy-led prototyping. Several audience members picked this up in the discussion.
key_points: Senckenberg has about 900 staff, eight research institutions and seven locations; SDMC implements DINA for all of them.
SDEI was founded in 1886 in Berlin, joined Senckenberg in 2009 and has about 35 people including volunteers.
Four of five sub-collections use Corel Paradox instances (from the 1990s) on individual computers; one manager keeps a card catalogue backup and another uses personal spreadsheets.
Schemas have diverged as managers added, moved and renamed fields; practices like putting subspecies in the species field hinder sharing.
There is no formal data governance or ownership, and decision power varies between technical assistants and scientific heads.
Her role: data life cycle documentation, legacy structure assessment, training, liaison with SDMC, and workflows for enrichment, mapping and migration.
Treating work as prototypes (design thinking) and letting specialists test them builds ownership.

content_items.title: A framework for aligning collections data with the global data ecosystem from data creation to extension in the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History Department of Paleobiology

programme.title: A framework for aligning collections data with the global data ecosystem from data creation to extension in the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History Department of Paleobiology
programme.session: SYM29A From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract:
For many years, the biodiversity and geoscience informatics communities have worked together to establish a dynamic global data ecosystem that supports interdisciplinary and cutting-edge research. Natural history collections provide vital specimen-based data that are foundational for this ecosystem. While informatics communities expand data across this landscape by developing new concepts, data models, standards, and more, collections are challenged to move beyond baseline data practices and keep pace with evolving data needs.

The Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History Department of Paleobiology (NMNH Paleo) recently launched a multi-year program to create an integrated framework that addresses enhancements in our data capture and processing, ultimately enabling a more robust local data ecosystem that can adapt to global developments. To achieve this goal, we will evaluate the best methods for implementing results from work by the broader community throughout our processes, creating data that can be extended or integrated with new sources and made more actionable and open for broader use. This initiative will also synthesize components of disparate projects, leveraging practices refined over many years across the biodiversity informatics and paleontology collections communities, as well as through recent cyberinfrastructure evaluation projects. Importantly, our work will be supported by a cross-functional team, incorporating a variety of expertise and perspectives to inform this framework. While our primary focus is on the NMNH Paleo collections, this integrated approach is intended to be adaptable to other paleontology collections and likely other natural history collections.

speakers.name: Holly Little
speakers.affiliation: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Department of Paleobiology

actual.identification_notes: Speaker self-introduced as Informatics Manager, NMNH Paleobiology; content matches the abstract. Includes Q&A up to the transition to the panel discussion.

content_items.summary: Holly Little presented the Paleobiology department's new five-year, gift-funded 'paleo digital framework' for the world's largest fossil collection. The collection holds about 42 million objects, 800,000 records, and needs an estimated 10–13 million records. The framework covers the data life cycle from capture to enhancement, extension and publishing. It uses imaging-first capture, adaptable specimen surveys for core data points, material entity type and MIDS, and verbatim preservation before AI text extraction. It also aligns taxonomy and geological context with external sources and feeds corrections back to them, and uses Darwin Core Data Package profiles. The informatics team grows from one person to five. She asked the community for workflows and challenges to test.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Making paleo collections work in the global data ecosystem needs an iterative, full life-cycle framework, not one-off digitisation.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a concrete institutional roadmap for implementing years of community standards work (material entity type, DwC-DP, geological context). The team explicitly offers to pilot and share solutions.
key_points: A 2018 analysis showed low use of Darwin Core terms in paleo collections due to misunderstandings, missing terms and unlinkable resources.
The NMNH Paleobiology collection has about 42 million objects and about 800,000 records; an estimated 10–13 million records are needed.
The informatics team was one person until 2025, then two, with three more staff funded by a gift for a five-year project around 1,000 significant objects.
Principles: work iteratively, image first, share data widely and often, don't wait for perfection, align with global standards and FAIR.
Capture only core data points per specimen type and reuse ledgers (e.g. a locality shared by thousands of specimens) instead of re-transcribing labels.
Enhancement aligns taxonomy (WoRMS, Paleobiology Database, Catalogue of Life) and geological context with external sources and feeds issues back.
DwC-DP mapping showed that different publishing profiles suit different material types (e.g. organism relationships vs cores crossing horizons).
methods: AI text extraction with verbatim preservation
questions: What workflows from other institutions could be adapted?
What paleo data challenges remain unsolved?

content_items.title: Drawers in the dark harboring data that could spark - finding the sweet spot in collection digitization and mobilizing metadata from museum's collections

programme.title: Drawers in the dark harboring data that could spark - finding the sweet spot in collection digitization and mobilizing metadata from museum’s collections
programme.session: SYM29B From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract: Natural history museum’s collections have a long history in collecting, storing and giving access to an - usually - science-based community. But in today’s technologically connected society, there is expectation for access to data instantaneously. Traditional museums are taking up the journey to open up and make their collections publicly available to all. With this in mind, the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin started an action Plan in 2020 with the goal of digitizing all of the approximately 30 million collection objects in 10 years’ time. Since then, collection-, digitization-, media-and database managers work together and explore different formats and scales of project workflows. Here we examine how museum collections can move from slow and fragmented efforts to a scalable and integrated strategy. We argue why aiming for perfection in every digital record slows down the digital transformation. This tradeoff between slowly acquired high quality, “gold standard” digital assets and a straight forward interoperable dataset with FAIR data needs to be managed. In the end, museums must decide when perfection slows the trail, and when “good enough” leads to collections that spark and knowledge that’s shines at scale.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by Caitlin Thorn ('Nora Linke-Mass' in ASR); content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Nora Lentge-Maaß described MfN's state-funded plan to digitise about 30 million objects holistically: condition assessment, conservation, inventory, digitisation and preparation for the move to a new building. Four digitisation managers and five scan operators were hired. Her showcase was DORA, a malacology digitisation station built with Fraunhofer IAO. It has four cameras with focus stacking, reads QR codes and outputs JSON metadata, and has processed about 170,000 of 260,000 lots (about 85% disclosed). A 2023 cyber attack took systems offline until July 2024 and forced reorganisation into a digitisation-on-demand office, the DCI team and an innovation lab. The lab's new Fides station images insects from several angles. Her take-home: plan for the easy 95%.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Plan digitisation for the easy 95%, capture a minimal dataset, and decide when good enough beats perfection.
content_items.why_it_matters: It gives practical lessons from one of the largest museum digitisation programmes, including recovery from a cyber attack, with transferable guidance on minimal datasets and workflow design.
key_points: MfN's holistic approach combined condition assessment, conservation, inventory, digitisation, QA and new storage, driven by user demand.
Holdings were split into four categories with dedicated digitisation managers; 80% of objects were in historical cabinets.
DORA station: four built-in cameras, focus-stacked tray images with colour chart and scale, label capture, QR-code file naming, and JSON metadata output.
About 170,000 of about 260,000 malacology lots (about 7 million objects) processed; about 85% of the collection disclosed by 19 September.
A 2023 cyber attack destroyed back-end systems; MfN was offline from October 2023 to July 2024.
New structure: coordination office for digitisation on demand (with a request form), the digital catalogue infrastructure (Specify, media repository, data portal) and an innovation lab (ELIO).
The Fides station (with a small company) uses consumer cameras and multi-angle imaging for entomology, but captures media only; AI label transcription runs separately.

notable_claims.claim: About 170,000 malacology lots have been processed with DORA, disclosing roughly 85% of the collection.
The museum was completely offline from October 2023 until July 2024 after a severe cyber attack.
Plan digitisation efforts for the easy 95% and not the problematic 5%.

recommendations: Plan for the easy 95%, not the problematic 5%.
Collect as much metadata as possible but settle for a minimal dataset.
Use machine-readable aids to avoid naming errors.
Combine digitisation with inventory or move preparation.
Prefer online-based tools over local ones.
results_findings: About 85% of MfN malacology disclosed via DORA-based workflows.
limitations: Photographic digitisation was interrupted by the cyber attack, so not all processed lots have images.
Very large and very small objects remain slow and are handled mainly on request.

q_and_a.answer_summary: DNA sampling is a separate process with a DNA bank, to be integrated in a separate Specify instance; not yet combined with digitisation.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Stations target the medium-sized 95%; elephant skulls and 2–3 m trace fossils were photographed but are slow and done mostly on request.

content_items.title: Accelerating specimen identification through Virtual Collections while promoting collaboration

programme.title: Accelerating specimen identification through Virtual Collections while promoting collaboration
programme.session: SYM29B From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract:
Natural science collections are essential benchmarks for biodiversity research. Accelerating digitization highlights the need for taxonomic identification at scale, which Virtual Reference Collections (VRCs) provide by gathering expert-identified digital specimens. Funded by the TETTRIs project, we implemented VRCs into the DiSSCo infrastructure. By utilizing Persistent Identifiers (PIDs), VRCs ensure a stable reference to these digital objects, enabling reliable data citation and global collaboration. Consequently, users can seamlessly consult data and taxonomic experts can identify specimens remotely.

However, implementing effective VRCs requires addressing critical data challenges. Foremost, specimens must be expertly curated to ensure accuracy. Data must not remain siloed across separate portals; a VRC requires a single, user-friendly entry point. High-quality imagery is mandatory since standard digitization often misses diagnostic traits. Furthermore, these collections must represent complete taxonomic groups and meet machine-readable FAIR standards, including complete event dates and unique identifiers.

Supported by TETTRIs, DiSSCo addresses these hurdles by leveraging Digital Specimen architecture. Virtual Collections harmonize federated data into unified reference sets. Using PIDs and standardized schemas, experts aggregate specimens into citable, stable sets. This facilitates "curation-at-distance," allowing taxonomists to remotely validate and enrich metadata, bridging the gap between physical repositories and global expertise. In this session, we present DiSSCover’s new capabilities for creating and maintaining VRCs to solve these identified issues.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the chair; the speaker is a software developer on DiSSCo's Disscover platform. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Melanie de Leeuw showed how the DiSSCo platform Disscover is turning from a passive lookup tool into an active workspace through Virtual Reference Collections (VRCs), funded by TETTRIs. VRCs pool digital specimens from multiple institutions into one virtual drawer. Three use cases were given: remote curation (e.g. Naturalis hawk moths identified only to family), expert-validated machine-learning training sets, and virtual field guides for rare taxa. Each VRC gets a DOI, aggregates across institutions, keeps two-way specimen–collection relationships, and supports expert annotation. Screenshots of the acceptance environment showed public browsing and ORCID-authenticated creation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Virtual reference collections with DOIs let experts identify and curate dispersed digital specimens remotely instead of shipping material or travelling.
content_items.why_it_matters: It turns existing digitised specimens into a collaborative identification resource and suggests a route to citable ML training data. It also raises the unresolved question of feeding annotations back to physical collections.
key_points: Taxonomy is stuck in a cycle: physical distance limits experts, and digitised data stuck in silos doesn't help.
VRCs pool digital specimens from institutions such as Naturalis, London, Paris and Oslo into one workspace.
Use cases: curation at a distance, ML training datasets, and virtual field guides for rare or fragile taxa.
Four pillars: a DOI per VRC, cross-institutional aggregation, dynamic entity relationships and active remote curation.
Browsing is open without login; creating a VRC requires ORCID login and an appropriate role.
Next steps: user-group involvement, VRC modification while preserving stability, and an annotation validation framework.

notable_claims.claim: Every virtual reference collection is assigned a DOI, making it a permanent, citable scientific asset.
No virtual collections are yet in production; the demonstration used the acceptance environment.

limitations: Datasets vary in whether they have images; the examples shown were deliberately chosen.
No validated workflow yet for updating physical collections after online annotations.
future_work: Allow modification of virtual collections while keeping them stable.
Annotation validation framework (possibly next year).
examples_case_studies: Naturalis Sphingidae (hawk moths) identified only to family.
Pyralidae specimens as an ML training-set illustration.
Virtual field guide for fragile rare fossils dispersed across European museums.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Not yet known; circulating enriched data back to sources digitally is being worked on, and the question will go to user groups and Naturalis.

content_items.title: Managing high-volume specimen movements in the entomological collection of Naturalis with a new type of record

programme.title: Managing high-volume specimen movements in the entomological collection of Naturalis with a new type of record
programme.session: SYM29B From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract: The entomological, pinned collection at Naturalis contains approximately 1.7M specimens, of which about 10% are digitized. Collection managers mostly use a higher level of data (the storage units) to retrieve and manage the collection. The physical storage units contain multiple taxa, which is reflected in the storage unit record as multiple identifications. New acquisitions and taxonomic reshuffling would cause collection managers to have to move the specimens of several taxa to adjacent storage units, and to remove an identification and reenter the data in the destination storage unit record. Given the high curation activity in entomology, this created a critical workload bottleneck with high risk for errors. At first, investigations were done to make identifications a separate subrecord, to allow moving between two storage units more easily. This was deemed too disruptive to the database architecture. Instead a new type of record was developed: the lot, a conceptual bridging entity. The lot record reflects an aggregation of specimens belonging to the same lowest-determined taxon stored within a contiguous physical location. It can be connected to a specific storage unit, optimizing digital workload following physical actions. Also, in the future it will be easier to publish this data at short intervals (as opposed to the static dataset of storage units which is now 8 years old). Ultimately, this implementation satisfies the most frequent inquiries from both external and internal users: confirming whether a specific taxon is present in the Naturalis collection, and pinpointing exactly where it is stored.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Merian van Bossem' and later addressed as 'Miriam' (ASR for Myriam van Walsum); she is system owner of the collection management applications at Naturalis. Content matches the abstract. No questions were asked.

content_items.summary: Myriam van Walsum explained a workload problem in Naturalis's pinned insect collection (about a third of 45 million specimens, only about 10% individually digitised). Records exist mainly at drawer level, with a table of identifications per storage unit. When taxa shifted between drawers, staff had to delete and manually re-enter identifications, so moves were often not recorded. Instead of disruptive independent taxon records, Naturalis introduced a 'lot' record: specimens of the same lowest determined taxon stored in one contiguous location. It is created by migrating existing storage-unit records, so moving a taxon only means updating the lot's link. A Catalogue of Life API lookup also reduced entry errors. She asked how lots should map to Darwin Core or DwC-DP and whether GBIF or DiSSCo want such records.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A 'lot' record linking taxa to storage units makes high-volume physical moves cheap to record and tells staff where each taxon is.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a practical data-model fix for a common curation bottleneck in drawer-level digitised collections. It also raises an open standards question about publishing lot and storage-unit records.
key_points: Naturalis holds about 45 million specimens; over a third are pinned insects, only about 10% individually digitised (mostly bees).
The zoology/geology CMS is from a Dutch vendor not designed for natural history, so Naturalis writes its own ABCD-aligned requirements.
Taxonomically ordered storage creates many-to-many relationships between taxa and storage units.
Manual delete/re-enter of identifications caused backlog, errors and lost locations, despite a legal obligation to know where specimens are.
Lot definition: specimens of the same lowest determined taxon in one contiguous location; each specimen belongs to exactly one lot.
Lots were created by data migration from existing storage-unit records; no new digitisation was needed.
Catalogue of Life API integration in identifications reduced data entry errors.
questions: How problematic will differing definitions of 'lot' be?
How should lots map to Darwin Core Archive or Darwin Core Data Package?
Is there a use case for lot/storage-unit records in Disscover or GBIF?

notable_claims.claim: Only about 10% of Naturalis's pinned insect specimens are individually digitised; the rest are digitised at drawer level.
Moving a taxon to another drawer now requires only updating the lot's relationship link.
Implementing the Catalogue of Life API in identifications reduced data entry errors.

results_findings: Simplified movement workflow and satisfied collection managers.
limitations: Naturalis still publishes a static drawer dataset created over eight years ago on GBIF.
future_work: Publish a live lot-based dataset once the mapping question is resolved.

content_items.title: Everything is coded: How to prevent a game of telephone in a system full of interfaces

programme.title: Everything is coded: How to prevent a game of telephone in a system full of interfaces
programme.session: SYM29B From Cabinets to Clouds - Bridging the gap between collection- and database management
programme.abstract:
Building a basic data infrastructure for a digital collection is not a particularly cutting-edge project, although, of course, there are many design decisions to be made that have a major impact on the system’s performance, interoperability, and resilience. However, such projects typically do not start from scratch but evolve within socio-technical environments whose subsystems are characterized by huge differences, particularly with regard to digital literacy as well as in terms of understanding scientific methods and the significance of research data. In our case, this is particularly relevant for the involvement of natural and social scientists, collection managers, project coordinators, technical developers, and data users in exhibition and education.

Designing cross-disciplinary processes for the generation, transformation, and publication of specimen-related data faces various challenges under these circumstances. For example, interfaces are needed throughout the entire data pipeline where translations must take place: from unstructured to structured forms, from human-readable to machine-readable, from one professional group’s specialized terminology to another’s, and from strategic thinking to actual agile development work.

In our presentation, we’ll use specific examples to demonstrate how successfully - or unsuccessfully - we manage to transfer data from one expert to another, while on the one hand preserving the essential integrity and significance of the information across all transformation steps, and on the other hand building trust among stakeholders for whom parts of the infrastructure are inevitably a black box.

actual.identification_notes: Programmed speaker Franziska Schuster co-presented with developer Jasper (introduced as 'Jasper Funk Smid'), who is not listed in the programme. The chair said 'Present' for 'Prevent' in the title. Includes Q&A.

content_items.summary: Franziska Schuster framed MfN's digital catalogue infrastructure work through the 'game of telephone': standard formats like Darwin Core alone don't keep data meaning intact across professional hand-offs. Developer Jasper then described migrating about 600,000 insect specimen records with 2.5 million images, digitised by a Picturae conveyor pipeline, into Specify after the cyber attack fragmented the data. Requirements unclear from the start made his mapping code slow and hard to verify. Taxon 'NURIs' (internal identifiers) turned out to be non-unique, with up to 2,000 IDs for one taxon, test entries and drawer IDs reused as taxon IDs. Schuster closed with Scrum as a 'don't panic' strategy with three-week sprints and stakeholder feedback.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Shared understanding of what data means must be established at the start of a pipeline; standard formats alone won't stop meaning drifting between people.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a candid case study of how identifier semantics break down in mass digitisation pipelines, and it shows how agile methods can manage infrastructure rebuilds.
key_points: Coded systems narrow meaning only if sender and receiver share an understanding of the code.
The Picturae conveyor pipeline digitised just over 600,000 specimens with over 2.5 million images, about 5,000 specimens per day, over roughly 2.5 years including development.
After the hack the data were fragmented; deduplication and consolidation came before mapping to Specify.
Iterative feedback from Specify and collection managers made the mapping code increasingly slow and opaque; a month-long rewrite followed after publishing about 22,000 records.
Taxon NURIs were not unique: up to 2,000 IDs per taxon, empty taxa with IDs, and test entries.
Pragmatic fix: accept a taxon NURI only if unique; otherwise keep it in the determination for findability.
Key missing question: is the data sufficient at this point to assign an identifier?
Scrum with prioritised backlogs (must/should/could/won't) and three-week sprints with stakeholder feedback helps the team avoid panic.
questions: When is data sufficient to assign a persistent identifier?

notable_claims.claim: Some taxonomic entities had up to 2,000 supposedly unique taxon identifiers.
Drawer identifiers were used as taxon identifiers under time pressure.
After the attack MfN chose a cloud-hosted Specify, leading to a closer relationship with the Specify consortium.
The conveyor pipeline ran at about 5,000 specimens per day.

recommendations: Establish a common understanding of data meaning at the start of pipeline design.
Consider whether data are sufficient before assigning identifiers.
Use a database from the start.
limitations: Documentation of the original identifier process was largely nonexistent, and the hack destroyed some context.

q_and_a.question: Were the issues mainly due to lack of preparation? (Smithsonian, which uses the same conveyor system)
q_and_a.answer_summary: There was much preparation, but implementation involved improvised decisions and a poorly understood strategic push; no CMS was running at the time to receive data directly.

q_and_a.question: How long did digitising 600,000 specimens take, and did the cyber attack help consolidate systems?
q_and_a.answer_summary: About two and a half years including co-development with Picturae; the attack prompted a cloud-hosted approach with the Specify consortium, though starting from scratch risks over-engineering.

representative_excerpt.text: So we heard it's really important to make clear at the beginning of the design of the process that we have a common understanding of the meaning of the data, which is also very important because the collection management has to trust this infrastructure because they have to give away their data and kind of lose some of their control over it.

content_items.title: From Specimens to Networks: Darwin Core Data Packages in Practice

programme.title: From Specimens to Networks: Darwin Core Data Packages in Practice
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract: This year the Darwin Core standard gained a Conceptual Model and a Data Package guide detailing its practical application. These additions represent significant semantic evolution and the capacity to integrate a greater variety of primary biodiversity data within and between datasets of biological collections. By moving beyond the Darwin Core Archive, with its inherent structural limitations, the model enables institutions to capture the depth and richness of specimen and associated data through material object hierarchies and relationships to Media, Nucleotide Analyses and Sequences, Surveys, and more. We will explore the implications for collection management systems and the practical challenges of mapping existing institutional data models into the relational structures enabled by the Darwin Core Data Package framework.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'John Maschke' (ASR error for John Wieczorek); content matches the abstract. He said he was listed as virtual but presented in person.

content_items.summary: John Wieczorek explained that Darwin Core has moved from a 'bag of terms' to a standard with a conceptual model defining relationships between classes, focusing on MaterialEntity. Material entities can be part of or derived from other material entities. They take part in collection, sampling and derivation events, serve as evidence for occurrences and identifications, and connect to geological context and chronometric age. They can also underpin nucleotide analyses and sequences. Agents, media, assertions, identifiers, references, provenance, protocols and usage policies attach to classes via role and link tables. He closed by demonstrating the Darwin Core Data Package Designer, which generates a datapackage.json from selected tables.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: The Darwin Core conceptual model and Data Package give material entities a rich, relational context that flat Darwin Core Archives could not express.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is the foundational explanation of DwC-DP semantics that several later talks in the session mapped against. The Designer tool offers a practical starting point for mapping CMS data.
key_points: Darwin Core was a 'bag of terms'; the conceptual model now adds semantics at the level of classes as part of the standard.
MaterialEntity: identifiable, persists for some time, consists wholly or partly of physical matter (organism, part, non-biological material, environmental sample).
Two self-referential relationships: part of (physically connected) and derived from (no longer connected).
Material entities take part in collecting, sampling and derivation (lab) events, and are evidence for occurrences and identifications.
Geological context and chronometric age separate today's collecting event from the inferred past occurrence.
Molecular data: material (even used-up material) is the basis for nucleotide analyses and sequences.
Agents (people, institutions, software/AI) link via role tables; media link via material-media and event-media tables; assertions generalise measurements or facts.
The Darwin Core Data Package Designer visualises relationships and generates a datapackage.json.

notable_claims.claim: The conceptual model is the first time a layer of semantics at the level of Darwin Core classes has been contributed as part of the standard.
MaterialEntity has two self-referential relationships: part-of and derived-from.
Geological context allows the collecting event today to be separated from the occurrence it infers in the past.

notable_moments.description: From 'bag of terms' to a conceptual model.

content_items.title: Aligning An Evolving Global Data Model To Software With Global Ambitions: GBIF x TaxonWorks

programme.title: Aligning An Evolving Global Data Model To Software With Global Ambitions: GBIF x TaxonWorks
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract: TaxonWorks (TW) has an implementation schema of over 70 models that it uses to facilitate the description of Earth's biodiversity. While it exports DarwinCore Occurrences and Checklists, Catalogue of Life Data Packages, and other standards its development was not constrained to those standards. As a proxy to the needs of a growing community of users it therefore acts as a lens to explore potential emerging standards. The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) is in the process of finalizing changes with respect to how they represent data under their umbrella via the DarwinCore Data Package framework. The new semantics introduced within DwC-DP create a clean space within which to compare TW concepts. Both models are strongly similar in how they seek to "shape" data, they strongly overlap conceptually. To identify the infrastructure changes required to efficiently export from TW to the DwC-DP standard, specifically to minimize data loss (all data-mappings are lossey to some degree) we map core concepts in both. We focus on 1) the interrelationship between DwC-DP's "Assertion" class and TW Observation and DataAttribute classes; 2) the nature of DwC Occurrences and related entities in TW (specifically the nature of "material" entities); and 3) abstractions related to the handling of annotations (e.g. Identifiers, Media). Some of our exploration has been facilitated by the Species File Group's "grand schema" and "SFGBorg" projects, internal efforts focused on data exchange and interoperability, we contextualize those efforts in this comparison. Finally, as potential fodder for future standards, we re-introduce the conceptual domains of Process and Rendering, and describe how TW is exploring development in these realms.

content_items.summary: Matt Yoder compared TaxonWorks' API-first data model with the new Darwin Core Data Package (DP). He found the conceptual overlap 'uncanny' after years of independent development. DP's many media, identifier, protocol and reference link tables collapse into single polymorphic annotation tables in TaxonWorks. TaxonWorks lacks a primary Survey concept and full nucleotide analysis, while DP lacks precise anatomy links and physical container hierarchies. He proposed recording mappings (broader/narrower) in SSSOM, merging them in RDF into a 'data mapping of all data mappings', and exposing /vocab endpoints. His observations: partial alignment and lossy exchange are the norm, both models have competing 'fuzzy buckets', and DP's role as an exchange format is unclear.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: TaxonWorks and DwC-DP have converged conceptually, but exchange between rich models will always be lossy, so mappings should be recorded explicitly.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a concrete software–standard alignment exercise with ideas (SSSOM mappings, /vocab endpoints) that could help many CMSs map to DwC-DP. It also flags practical issues like duplicate extension buckets.
key_points: TaxonWorks serves taxonomists first and now about 10–11 large collections; it is API-first and set up for human and agentic contributions.
It already offers Darwin Core import/export, a built-in IPT-like GBIF endpoint, EML persistence and lossless DwC import; an Orthoptera project round-tripped over a million GBIF records.
Conceptual overlap with DwC-DP is remarkable; TaxonWorks models one image depicting many concepts via a single annotation pattern.
Gaps in TaxonWorks: Survey as a primary concept, full nucleotide analysis; gaps in DP: precise anatomy, physical containers, loans, stronger geo-reference primacy.
Mappings can be expressed as broader/narrower relations and persisted in SSSOM, merged in RDF.
Both models have two 'buckets' for fuzzy data (resource relationship vs assertions; observations), which will confuse users.
Needs identified: equipment and configuration, experiments, genomes, more strongly typed agents; comments used as definitions cause confusion.
questions: Is DwC-DP intended as an exchange format, given the effort of mapping many models to many?
Is always-lossy exchange a barrier to describing life at scale?
Will SSSOM be adequate for schema exchange?
When and how will AI contribute meaningfully to concepts in these models?

content_items.title: Material Samples and Occurrences in Darwin Core Data Packages: Practical Experiences from DINA

programme.title: Material Samples and Occurrences in Darwin Core Data Packages: Practical Experiences from DINA
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
Research collection management systems (CMS) are the principal tools used to host and mobilize material sample data to biodiversity data infrastructures. The mobilization process traditionally depends on the export of the collection data in the Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) format. This data export often involves the flattening of information from complex relational structures and the synthetic generation of occurrences. The new Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) format provides an opportunity to overcome these limitations by (1) following a relational data model and (2) relaxing requirements so that valid Darwin Core data can also be transported without instantiating occurrences. However, new challenges arise from the alignment of local, material-focused CMS data models and the conceptual model powering DwC-DP. A prominent example is the treatment of organism attributes such as sex or life stage, which are grouped under the Occurrence class in DwC-DP as they possibly change over time. In a CMS, however, usually data about preserved specimens or material parts derived from them are managed, where these attributes do not change and are directly associated with the material entity. As a result, exporting this type of information from a CMS still requires the generation of occurrences, which raises the question if and how occurrence IDs should be generated.

In this talk, we will discuss practical examples of complex material entities stored in DINA, a collaboratively developed specimen and sample-based CMS, and how they can be serialized to DwC-DP. We also demonstrate how DINA’s data model with managed attributes and field extension features provides a native way to store standards-conformant data and dynamically adapt to evolving and emerging biodiversity data standards.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Jonas Grieb ('Dino' in ASR for DINA); content matches the abstract. Affiliation from Marije Timmermans' reference to her SDMC colleague.

content_items.summary: Jonas Grieb asked whether the Darwin Core conceptual model and DwC-DP fix a long-standing problem: CMSs that only hold material and event data have had to invent occurrences to publish to GBIF, producing unstable occurrence IDs. The DINA data model represents material object histories as material samples linked by processes and to collecting events, with organisms carrying determinations. Two worked examples showed good fit. A bat specimen, tissue and molecular extract chain maps to derivedFrom relationships. A mud shrimp and clam preserved together map to partOf relationships, though organism sex and life stage have no place on Material without creating an Occurrence. DINA therefore aims to publish DwC-DP without occurrences and let consumers such as GBIF derive them, which needs agreed conventions.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: DINA's material-sample model maps well to DwC-DP, so DINA wants to publish without synthetic occurrences and needs community conventions for consumers to derive them.
content_items.why_it_matters: It tests in practice whether DwC-DP ends the 'material entities are not occurrences' problem, and pinpoints the remaining gap (sex and life stage on material) and a governance question for GBIF.
key_points: A large share of GBIF records have material-entity bases of record (preserved, fossil specimens, material samples).
Generating occurrences from material data causes unstable identifiers and incomplete events.
DINA (consortium since 2014, governed by an MOU) models material samples, processes (collecting, subsampling, extraction) and organisms with determinations.
Derivation chains map cleanly to MaterialEntity with derivedFromMaterialEntity; open question whether only the parent needs an event link.
Mixed-organism samples map to partOf relationships, with some semantic blurriness.
Sex and life stage cannot be placed on Material; options are a synthetic Occurrence (not favoured), non-schema fields, or Material Assertions (discoverability concerns).
DINA plans to publish DwC-DP without occurrences.
methods: worked examples of derivation and part-of relationships
questions: Should every derived material entity repeat the collecting event link?
Where should sex and life stage go for material entities without occurrences?

notable_claims.claim: Material entities are not occurrences, and generating occurrences from material data causes problems with stable identifiers and missing events.
DINA's data model is widely aligned with the new Darwin Core conceptual model, including material lineage and mixed-organism material.
DINA aims to mobilise data as DwC-DP without occurrences and let consumers derive occurrences.

recommendations: Agree conventions between publishers of material data without occurrences and downstream consumers.
results_findings: Material lineage and mixed-organism samples from DINA can be represented in DwC-DP.
limitations: No slot for organism sex and life stage on Material in current Darwin Core without an Occurrence.
examples_case_studies: Fruit bat catalogued specimen → tissue in alcohol → molecular extract.
Mud shrimp and associated clam preserved in one crustacean sample.

notable_moments.description: Worked example: derivation chain from a bat specimen.
The sex and life stage problem for material without occurrences.
Publish DwC-DP without occurrences; conventions needed.

content_items.title: Sharing Extended Specimen Data from Symbiota Portals using Registered Extensions

programme.title: Sharing Extended Specimen Data from Symbiota Portals using Registered Extensions
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract: As both a collection management system (CMS) and aggregation software, Symbiota (https://symbiota.org/) faces compounding challenges of making extended specimen data easy to enter, manage, and re-use for research. Symbiota portals are designed to be user friendly for people of varying levels of database experience-from new students to professional data managers-underscoring the need to keep interfaces and data structures as simple and intuitive as possible. To address these challenges, Symbiota code designers have chosen the seemingly straightforward approach of aligning extended specimen data with registered extensions, e.g., Extended Measurement or Facts, Resource Relationship, and GGBN Material Sample. Here we will describe the timeline and current use of registered extensions in Symbiota portals, including the newest tools, challenges, and community implementations of these extensions.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video introduced by the chair; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Katie Pearson described how Symbiota, open-source software serving as both CMS and mini-aggregator, stores and shares extended specimen data. It underlies 60+ portals, about 52 hosted at the University of Kansas Symbiota Support Hub, used by over 2,000 collections. Keeping a low barrier to entry, Symbiota stays occurrence-centred but supports registered GBIF/Darwin Core extensions: multimedia, identifications, Extended Measurement or Fact, GGBN Material Sample, Alternative Identifiers and Resource Relationship. Examples include herbarium phenology captured in eMoF linked to ontologies, NEON's DNA and tissue subsample tracking, and the Carlquist project linking field notebooks and photos to specimens. The trade-off is that extended data can no longer go in one CSV upload.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Existing registered Darwin Core extensions met each of Symbiota's extended-specimen needs, so look for existing standards before inventing new ones.
content_items.why_it_matters: It shows how a widely used, low-barrier CMS can share richer extended specimen data via existing standards, immediately visible on GBIF.

Built-in publishing sends data directly to GBIF without an IPT.
Extended Measurement or Fact captured herbarium phenology without a new standard, using ontology IDs for types and values.
The Material Sample extension (mostly GGBN terms) is used heavily by NEON for DNA and tissue subsamples.
Identifiers concatenated in 'other catalog numbers' became a separate table aligned with the Alternative Identifiers extension.
Resource Relationship links specimens to other specimens or external resources, e.g. the Carlquist project's field photos and notebooks.
New import/export tools were needed; the single-CSV upload was discontinued in favour of standards alignment.

notable_claims.claim: Symbiota underlies about 60 or more portals used by over 2,000 collections.
Phenological data could be packaged within Extended Measurement or Fact without developing a new standard.
Extended data can no longer all be included in a single CSV upload.

recommendations: Look for existing standards before developing your own.
limitations: Tension between robustness and standards alignment on the one hand and user-friendliness on the other.

Challenges and the recommendation to reuse existing standards.

content_items.title: Diversity Workbench (DWB) as a Standards-Based Collection Management System for Heterogeneous Research Data and Biodiversity Data Mobilization

programme.title: Diversity Workbench (DWB) as a Standards-Based Collection Management System for Heterogeneous Research Data and Biodiversity Data Mobilization
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
Research collection management systems must support heterogeneous data, distributed workflows, and standards-based publication to enable interoperable and sustainable biodiversity data flows. At the Leibniz Institute for the Analysis of Biodiversity Change, Diversity Workbench (DWB) is the central platform for managing, standardizing, and publishing collection and project data across different sites. As a modular relational database system with multi-tenant capabilities and granular rights management, it supports the differing requirements of zoological, geological, palaeontological and mineralogical collections as well as diverse research projects.

DWB integrates data from internal and external sources through standardized and customizable import workflows, including its Import Wizard and API-based ingestion pipelines. These support collection digitization, project-based data capture, and laboratory-derived workflows such as metabarcoding. Its modular architecture enables collection-specific curation while maintaining a common institutional data framework.

Close collaboration among all stakeholders ensures data quality, semantic consistency, and domain-appropriate mappings. DWB bridges internal workflows and external biodiversity infrastructures. Data are prepared and published according to community standards, including ABCD via BioCASe and Darwin Core via the GBIF IPT, enabling dissemination to GBIF, GGBN, GFBio, and NFDI4Biodiversity. Stable CETAF identifiers and DiSSCo DOIs support FAIR and sustainable publishing.

We present DWB as a practical example of a research-oriented CMS that combines modularity, standards compliance, and sustainable publication workflows across the full data lifecycle.

content_items.title: From Client to App: Extending Diversity Workbench with REST and graphical web interfaces

programme.title: From Client to App: Extending Diversity Workbench with REST and graphical web interfaces
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
Diversity Workbench is a collection management system that supports the diverse requirements of managing biological and geological collections. The Leibniz Institute for the Analysis of Biodiversity Change uses the Diversity Workbench as its central collection database. The system is organized into modules for specific tasks, including DiversityCollection for the collection digitization, DiversityTaxonNames for taxonomy management, and DiversityProjects for project metadata administration. Each module uses its own relational SQL Server database and dedicated client software.

While this modular architecture enables highly flexible data management, it also results in complex desktop applications with limited transparency in user guidance and a dependency on Windows-based systems.

To address these limitations, we are developing two complementary components that use the existing relational databases as backend infrastructure: 1) a REST-compatible API that provides access to data in JSON, RDF, and HTML formats for machine interoperability, and 2) a configurable web application that allows users to focus on their specific data management tasks through graphical browser-based interfaces.

The API and web application are already being used in the upcoming version of our online collection catalog. In addition, the integration of the API into our ASV-Registry demonstrates its applicability beyond collection management, for example in specialized research domains such as metabarcoding data management. Together, these developments represent an important step toward improved usability, platform independence, and machine interoperability for Diversity Workbench.

content_items.title: Mapping the Relational Data Schema of the Diversity Workbench (DWB) to the Darwin Core Data Package Data Model to fit better to GBIF´s New Data Model

programme.title: Mapping the Relational Data Schema of the Diversity Workbench (DWB) to the Darwin Core Data Package Data Model to fit better to GBIF´s New Data Model
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
The publication workflow from the German Federation for Biological Data (GFBio) Data Centers at Natural History Collections to GBIF is relying on the BioCASe Provider Software and the ABCD standard. This approach emerged because the classical Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) model was often insufficient for representing complex relationships between collection objects, identifications, multimedia, agents, and related entities. However, the DWB-ABCD publication pathway also revealed some limitations within the GBIF ingestion workflow, as important dataset metadata, including multiple global identifiers, associated persons, institutions, and their roles, could not always be fully represented or displayed on the GBIF portal.

The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP), currently evolving within the GBIF and TDWG communities, aims to combine the strengths of both approaches. Aligned with the Darwin Core Conceptual Model and new ABCD versions, DwC-DP introduces a more flexible and semantically explicit framework for biodiversity data publishing.

This contribution presents a practical, AI-assisted mapping approach from DWB-based collection management software model to the emerging DwC-DP model. During the mapping process, information distributed across different DWB database modules is consolidated into DwC-DP entities while respecting existing relations, withhold settings and publication restrictions. Using real-world datasets from GFBio Data Center SNSB IT Center, we analyze how relational structures, identifiers, artefacts, material storage, agents and general metadata can be transformed into DwC-DP entities and properties.The results demonstrate the potential of DwC-DP for richer biodiversity data integration and improved metadata visibility within GBIF publishing workflows.

content_items.summary: Tanja Weibulat explained that GFBio data centres chose ABCD because early Darwin Core couldn't express DWB's complex relations. Their pipeline exports and filters DWB modules (withholding restricted data, anonymising people, rounding coordinates) into PostgreSQL, then maps to ABCD via BioCASe for GBIF and NFDI4Biodiversity. Limitations were that GBIF didn't display multiple identifiers, persons, roles or relations, and data papers needed manual entry. They prototyped mapping the same PostgreSQL tables to DwC-DP in a test IPT: observations and physical specimens split into Occurrence and Material, event, identification and agents shared, and analysis and processing combined into Material Assertion. Next steps are a GBIF sandbox comparison, metadata mapping and extending to the GFBio portal.

content_items.title: The More Extended, The More Open: Semantic Integration of 3D Natural Heritage Data into Biodiversity CMS

programme.title: The More Extended, The More Open: Semantic Integration of 3D Natural Heritage Data into Biodiversity CMS
programme.session: SYM42A Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
Biodiversity platforms are evolving into 'Open Knowledge Spaces' connecting primary data, research, and exploration. While the Digital Extended Specimen (DES) framework integrates derivative data, current Collection Management Systems (CMS) using models like openDS limit the ability to accommodate the 3D complexity and broader utility of physical specimens.

Mobilizing biodiversity data beyond taxonomy-into exhibitions, citizen science, and AI-requires high-fidelity 3D resources. For these to act as reliable knowledge assets, an expanded schema must track 3D modeling paradata and 'utilization contexts' of how specimens are preserved and exhibited. Through the temporal dynamics of human curation, biological specimens transform from mere evidence into 'Natural Heritage' with socio-historical value.

This study proposes a 'Natural Historical Specimen (NHS)' data model based on 3D data from 320 natural heritage animal species in South Korea. To maximize interoperability, this schema integrates Darwin Core (DwC) for occurrences, Prov-O and MorphoSource for 3D digitization provenance, and CIDOC-CRM for institutional curation and exhibition contexts.

Mapping biological resources, digital objects, and utilization contexts ensures traceability from field collection to public engagement. We implemented an interactive dashboard using this model, enabling users to explore morphological attributes and historical trajectories via a Knowledge Graph. This study offers practical solutions for next-generation CMS, demonstrating that integrating DwC and CIDOC-CRM standards elevates 3D resources into hubs within global biodiversity networks.
