content_items.summary: Yeeun Lee argued that specimens bridge natural history and heritage, because they record biological evidence along with histories of collection, curation, research and exhibition. Existing services (GBIF, BHL, Smithsonian 3D, DiSSCo) cover parts of the task in separate systems, and 3D data are often low quality. The project combines AI-assisted photogrammetric 3D capture of specimens from seven institutions, sized from insects to large mammals, with a semantic model of data, metadata and paradata layers. The model is aligned with openDS, Dublin Core, Europeana and CIDOC CRM, and visualised in Neo4j as a knowledge graph of about 2,400 nodes and 3,600 relations. Example applications are CMS integration, recommendations and map-based views.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Treating 3D specimen models as entry points in a knowledge graph that includes heritage context and digitisation paradata makes them reusable knowledge assets.
content_items.why_it_matters: It links biodiversity and cultural heritage standards and argues for recording 3D production paradata, which matters as 3D specimens are used for exhibitions, citizen science and AI.

Natural heritage information is distributed across institutions with differing quality, and 3D data are often low quality.

It is aligned with openDS, Dublin Core, Europeana and CIDOC CRM via one-to-one mappings.

content_items.title: Old habits and new visions: Exploring the RECODE data model, future integration and data enhancement

programme.title: Old habits and new visions: Exploring the RECODE data model, future integration and data enhancement
programme.session: SYM42B Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
The NHM London RECODE programme tasked with developing and implementing a new collections management system has been actively implementing since late 2023. With a vision of a sustainable and community focused system. RECODE has tackled a conscious shift to a more normalised data model and a focus on the use of bidirectional links to better represent and manage the NHM collections data and museum procedures.

In this talk we will share key insights into the new Doxis system, considerations around the developed data model and key functionality that we will leverage. As the system stabilises and data migration tests bring real data into the system the programme is also able to reflect on the impact of the data model and how it performs against the complexity, inconsistency and scale of NHM’s data.

Presentation points will include:

A complex object model that supports derived objects, groups, parts and preparations as a significant step indisambiguating objects from specimens and from collections management procedures.

In system access to the data model has provided better visibility of system databases, classes, fields, field types, relationships and configuration dependencies. The DM-viewer supports understanding the Doxis system and is expected to provide significant core functionality in terms of visualising data standards, search pathways, permissions and user insight into data structures.

Internal system data validation to support data integrity, quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) to support heterogeneous data and data standard constraints.

content_items.summary: Steen Dupont gave an update on NHM London's RECODE programme (since 2019) to replace a 20-year-old CMS, with go-live expected early next year on the Doxis platform. The data model was heavily normalised: about 70 object record types and 54,000 fields were reduced to about 6,500 in use and then 600–700 fields in four collection object entities (biological, geological, extraterrestrial, human-made). The new system uses true relationships, separates objects from processes, and enforces stricter taxonomy and location hierarchies. Videos of the UAT environment showed a data model viewer, agent relationships, a workflow engine (parallel acquisitions, sequential loans, silent movement control) and a bulk-ingest template builder that outputs CSV/JSON with dynamic errors.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Normalising decades of flat CMS data into relational entities and workflow-driven processes gives NHM a foundation for integrations and AI, but it needs institutional governance.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a rare look inside a large museum's CMS rebuild, with concrete numbers on field reduction and design choices other institutions can learn from.

content_items.title: The Unruliness of Higher Geography: What is it doing for us?

programme.title: The Unruliness of Higher Geography: What is it doing for us?
programme.session: SYM42B Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract:
In natural science collections, the concept of a collecting locality intermixes human and physical geography. This breadth is necessary to facilitate sharing location information, not only for research but also to ensure legal compliance and to encourage ethical practices. Geography is a primary facet for discovery and analysis of collections-based data, and we increasingly need ways to share geographic data accurately regardless of how precise it is. For example, a mollusk specimen collected from a given watershed in 2020 likely has location data that includes precise coordinates recorded from a GPS unit, and a mollusk specimen collected in 1920 may only have the watershed recorded, but either way, “watershed” may be the most useful concept. Geography is fluid, no matter what flavor of geography is being considered. Maps get redrawn and tectonic plates move, which means that geographic concepts are most useful when associated with time.

In this talk, we review existing conceptual models for capturing and sharing geographic information from common Collections Management Systems, data standards, and data aggregators. We then highlight pain points within these models, and illustrate their impact on discoverability. For example, although the “Atlantic Ocean” is a fundamental geographic concept, finding specimens that were collected in the Atlantic Ocean can be challenging. These pain points are connected by a throughline of forcing physical and administrative geographies together. We close by suggesting the need for a new TDWG task group under the Darwin Core Maintenance Group to assess the current terms and recommend modifications or additions.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video; Krimmel presents on behalf of herself and a colleague named Teresa, based on Arctos work but not an official Arctos position. Chair said she was filling in for a colleague.

content_items.summary: Erika Krimmel argued that Darwin Core's handling of higher geography is unruly. The dwc:higherGeography term is loosely defined and often a concatenation of other fields. Physical geography (oceans, drainage basins, mountain ranges) and many human regions (parks, EEZs, historical countries) lack explicit terms. A US freshwater mussel study used only georeferenced records and so missed 51% of the data, even though many historic records named drainages precisely enough for the question. GBIF indexes higherGeography and waterBody as text, so finding Atlantic Ocean records takes several searches. Boundary changes over time (Valencia/Cibola County, New Mexico) add confusion. She proposed a Darwin Core Maintenance Group task group.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Darwin Core needs more explicit, time-aware ways to share human and physical geography so data without coordinates can still be discovered and used.
content_items.why_it_matters: Much historic specimen data can't be georeferenced but has meaningful higher geography. Better terms could unlock it for conservation research.
key_points: Higher geography contextualises localities and is a useful first-pass filter.
dwc:higherGeography is open to interpretation and becomes a 'trash basket or treasure trove'.
Physical geography is treated much less explicitly than human geography in Darwin Core.
Freshwater mussel study: 51% of records (ungeoreferenced historic specimens, including a holotype) were excluded despite having drainage information.
GBIF indexes higherGeography and waterBody as text strings, so concept-based search (e.g. Atlantic Ocean) needs several queries.
Geography changes over time (e.g. Cibola County carved from Valencia County in 1981), so concepts are most useful with a time.
questions: What belongs in dwc:higherGeography?
Which time-stamp of higher geography should be used?
How can aggregators consider records without coordinates?

notable_claims.claim: A freshwater mussel study missed 51% of the data because it could only use georeferenced specimens.
GBIF indexes higherGeography and waterBody as text strings rather than concepts.
Aggregating Atlantic Ocean records on GBIF currently needs at least four searches.

recommendations: Form a task group under the Darwin Core Maintenance Group on higher geography terms, vocabularies and IRI terms.
examples_case_studies: Lewis River, Oregon holotype: too imprecise to georeference but adequate for drainage-level analysis.
Toad record collected in Valencia County now falls in Cibola County per GADM.

representative_excerpt.text: The moral here, we're missing 51% of the data in this study with real conservation implications, and many of the specimens left out are arguably the most important

notable_moments.description: Freshwater mussel study and drainage as the unit of analysis.
Searching GBIF for the Atlantic Ocean.

content_items.title: Mobilizing rich, interoperable, and secure fossil data from underserved collections using Symbiota

programme.title: Mobilizing rich, interoperable, and secure fossil data from underserved collections using Symbiota
programme.session: SYM42B Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges
programme.abstract: Symbiota software underlies over 70 data portals that are used as collections management systems and data aggregators. While U.S. federal funding catalyzed the use of Symbiota for the digitization of biological collections, Symbiota’s uptake by the paleontological community was previously limited by a lack of functionality for paleontological context data. To address these needs, new software enhancements for managing and publishing fossil specimen data are now available in Symbiota 3.4. Notably, these enhancements implement full functionality for Darwin Core GeologicalContext terms in Symbiota’s public interfaces, at the database level, and for data harvesting. Substantial development efforts have been leveraged to reconfigure the handling of chronostratigraphic information to align output data with GBIF’s GeoTime vocabulary and improve downstream interoperability. These features are complemented by revised documentation available in the Symbiota Docs user information resource and via a new Paleo Data Knowledge Hub. In addition to making these enhancements available to all Symbiota portals, a new Symbiota portal, the “Paleo Data Portal” (PDP), was launched to provide secure infrastructure to fossil collections that have not yet received support through U.S. federal digitization funding, allowing these collections to engage in the global paleo data ecosystem. The PDP currently serves as a testing ground to better understand gaps in existing data standards and digitally available taxonomy to inform a forthcoming “Paleo Roadmap” intended to guide future paleo-related cyberinfrastructure improvements. All Symbiota software enhancements are synergistic with greater community-wide efforts to improve the utility of existing cyberinfrastructure for paleontological research.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video presented on behalf of project lead Lindsay Walker; developers named as 'Nikita Salakov' and Ed Gilbert (ASR). Co-authors Holly Little and Talea were said to be at the conference.

content_items.summary: Erika Krimmel described a project (started 2023) to make Symbiota work for fossil collections, which are underrepresented despite Symbiota's popularity with small, under-resourced collections. A new Paleo Data Portal serves as testbed. Enhancements released in Symbiota 3.4 include GBIF GeoTime–based chronostratigraphy entry with auto-populated hierarchy, and staging scripts for stratigraphic and morphology remarks. There is inclusive numerical-time search, a Macrostrat geology map layer (also in georeferencing), and taxonomy sourced from Catalogue of Life XR via ChecklistBank to trace errors. Other additions: default 'FossilSpecimen' basis of record, description fields for material type, and relationships such as part/counterpart and slab-with. Features are documented in Symbiota Docs and a new Paleodata Knowledge Hub, and collections are being onboarded.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Targeted Symbiota enhancements around geological context, taxonomy and relationships make a low-barrier CMS viable for under-resourced fossil collections.
content_items.why_it_matters: It extends the benefits of a widely used, low-cost platform to paleontological collections and improves how geological time data reach GBIF.
key_points: Symbiota's pre-2023 paleo module had undocumented custom fields, and geological context was not searchable or exportable publicly.
Chronostratigraphic entry now uses a controlled vocabulary aligned with GBIF GeoTime and the International Chronostratigraphic Chart.
Search over geological time is inclusive using the vocabulary's numerical timescale, based on researcher feedback.
Macrostrat API geology layer is available in map search and georeferencing.
Taxonomy is sourced from Catalogue of Life Extended Release in ChecklistBank, allowing tracing and reporting of incorrect higher taxonomy.
Collections can set FossilSpecimen as the default basis of record.
Relationships document part/counterpart pairs and slab associations with uncatalogued material; links to MorphoSource, MorphoBank and BHL.

notable_claims.claim: Symbiota was reconfigured to use a controlled vocabulary aligned with GBIF GeoTime, itself aligned with the International Chronostratigraphic Chart.
Searches spanning geological time intervals are inclusive, not literal, drawing on the vocabulary's numerical timescale.

results_findings: Existing portals (the 'Tridaphite Collections Consortium' as transcribed, Cretaceous Vertebrates of Madagascar, International Taphonomy Reference Collection) benefited immediately.
future_work: Continue onboarding collections to the Paleo Data Portal.

notable_moments.description: Chronostratigraphy via GBIF GeoTime vocabulary.
Taxonomy from Catalogue of Life XR via ChecklistBank.
Part/counterpart and slab-with relationships.

content_items.title: SYM42 discussion: DwC-DP profiles, deriving occurrences, ABCD's future and system boundaries

programme.title: Discussion
programme.session: SYM42B Solutions for Research Collection Management Systems Challenges

actual.identification_notes: Scheduled discussion moderated by James Macklin and Jonas Grieb, starting with questions from the Whova chat. Several audience speakers are unnamed; one is addressed as 'Nicky'. 'York Poland' is likely ASR for Jorrit Poelen.

content_items.summary: Wieczorek answered a chat question on registering DwC-DP profiles (e.g. a GBIF profile requiring occurrences): none exist yet, but community-created, community-vetted profiles could become standard products. Grieb discussed who should derive occurrences, and a GBIF participant asked what rules GBIF should follow; the panel called for community-driven, rule-based conventions. Weibulat said German data centres must still decide on ABCD's future. Dupont confirmed RECODE's strong API. Yoder noted agentic pull requests from students and the public, and Macklin reflected on how far CMSs should manage links versus rely on external services. Participants suggested core-versus-plugin architectures, and Yoder warned most links die within ten years.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Richer relational models bring the community together but raise hard governance questions about profiles, occurrence derivation, system scope and link persistence.
content_items.why_it_matters: It captures open design questions for the DwC-DP transition and for CMS architecture as AI-assisted development and linked services grow.
key_points: There are no DwC-DP profiles now because early feedback asked for a single model, but communities have since asked for tailored profiles.

The latest Darwin Core public review incorporated GBIF cores and simple extensions (measurement or fact, identification history, alternative identifiers, Humboldt, chronometric age) into the standard; OBIS and GGBN extensions await conversations.
DINA would prefer to publish without occurrences and let GBIF derive them if technically feasible.
GBIF asked whether derivation should use explicit flags or rule-based logic (e.g. event + identification + material).
German NFDI data centres still use ABCD and must decide whether to switch.
Agentic coding creates a flood of pull requests; semantic-layer changes need strict control, UI changes less so.
Suggestion to separate core from blessed plug-ins to manage community contributions.
Link rot: most links don't last longer than ten years, so systems must decide what to persist locally.
questions: Should the Darwin Core Maintenance Group maintain a registry of named DP profiles, and how would they be governed?
Wouldn't publishers prefer to control what becomes an occurrence rather than leave it to GBIF?
What rules should GBIF follow to derive occurrences from DwC-DP?
Is there still a use case for ABCD?
How far should a CMS manage linked data itself versus rely on external services?

notable_claims.claim: There are currently no DwC-DP profiles; only one model exists.
GBIF cores and several simple extensions were incorporated into the Darwin Core standard in the latest public review.
Most links will not last longer than ten years.

recommendations: DP profiles should be created and vetted by the community like other standard components.
Communities needing specific extensions should work together and with GBIF.
Separate core system functionality from approved plug-ins to handle contribution volume.

q_and_a.question: Might the Darwin Core Maintenance Group produce a registry of named DP profiles, and how would they be governed?
q_and_a.answer_summary: No profiles or infrastructure exist yet; community-created, community-vetted profiles could be added as standard products.

q_and_a.question: Wouldn't you prefer to control what becomes an occurrence rather than leave it to GBIF?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Conceptually DINA prefers separating occurrences from material; if GBIF allows material-only publication and derives occurrences, DINA would use that, subject to technical feasibility.

q_and_a.question: What rules should GBIF follow to derive occurrences?
q_and_a.answer_summary: No firm answer; community-driven conventions are needed; a rule-based approach (material plus event) is worth exploring.

q_and_a.question: Is there still a use case for ABCD?
q_and_a.answer_summary: German data centres currently publish ABCD and must discuss the future; the DwC-DP test will inform the decision.

notable_moments.description: Registry and governance of DwC-DP profiles.
GBIF asks what rules to use when deriving occurrences.
Agentic development and controlling the semantic layer.
Macklin on relationships and how far systems should go.
Link rot: most links don't last ten years.
